introduction.text: The Catacombs of Santa Felicita are a three‑level underground burial complex in Rome that illustrate early Christian burial practices and the evolving veneration of martyrs.

history.description: The edict of Milan in 313 made Christianity legal, after which the catacombs were first recorded under the name of Felicitas of Rome.
Pope Boniface I (418‑422) built a small underground basilica dedicated to Silanus and an above‑ground oratory for Felicitas, and was buried in a semi‑underground tomb on the site.
In the late 7th or early 8th century, a fresco depicting Felicitas surrounded by her seven children was found in the small basilica.
Pope Leo III translated Felicitas’ remains to Santa Susanna in the early 9th century, leading to the catacomb’s gradual abandonment.
In the 17th century the catacombs were also known as the Catacomb of Sant’Antonio after the Vienne monastery that owned the land.
The catacombs were rediscovered at the end of the 18th century after a crumbling building collapsed.
Giovanni Battista de Rossi’s 19th‑century excavations confirmed the catacombs belonged to Felicitas.
In 1884 a late 7th or early 8th‑century picture of Felicitas with her seven children was found in the small basilica.

design.description: A small underground basilica dedicated to Silanus, featuring an altar with his remains.
An above‑ground oratory dedicated to Felicitas, with a semi‑underground tomb for Pope Boniface I.
The catacombs consist of three levels of burial chambers carved into the subsoil.

art.description: A late 7th or early 8th‑century fresco depicting Felicitas surrounded by her seven children, found in the small basilica.
